extracted.intended_audience: students, historians, and general readers interested in the history and critique of advertising practices
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and cataloguing of historical advertising frauds, hoaxes, and deceptive practices as exemplified in 18th–19th century print advertisements and handbills. The page describes types of fraudulent ads, how they operated, and social effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid occult/mystic advertisements (wondrous arts)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'WONDROUS ARTS. — Your future revealed — Seven years, six stamps; lifetime twelve stamps. State age. Love Charn? sixteen stamps. Medicine for removing Gravel and Private diseases in a few days, without injuring the constitution, sixty stamps. Methralton's Bible Key, twenty-six stamps. Book of Spirits, 408 pages, thirty-two stamps. Millennial Prophecies, Gratis. Methralton, the Seer, Daventry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of an advert selling occult/mystical services and miracle remedies for payment by postage stamps. The text treats these offers as swindles that 'interfere with the matter' and prey on credulous readers; shows the pattern of listing multiple sensational products/prizes with small payment requirements (stamps) to solicit money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake stage/employment advertisements requiring fees
rubrics_metrics.description: THE STAGE.— WANTED, TWELVE LADIES and GENTLE- MEN (ages 16 to 40) for salaried engagements. Totally inexperienced persons may apply. — Communicate, by letter only, enclosing photograph and thirteen stamps, Histrionicus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers offering salaried acting engagements in return for fee/photograph/stamps. The page treats these as swindles that either cheat the applicants (mostly poor, helpless girls) or deceive the public about actual talent on the stage; highlights the form ('by letter only', fee in stamps/photograph) as characteristic of the scam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion-in-absentia / sham degree granting
rubrics_metrics.description: PROMOTION IN ABSENTIA.— Qualified surgeons, chemists, dentists, oculists, chiropodists, and professors of music or arts aspiring to a doctor's degree, may communicate by letter to Professor .
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sale of academic/professional degrees by mail ('promotion in absentia') where 'any one who liked to pay could obtain the most honourable degree'. The text documents the social harm: sham degree-holders become indistinguishable in presentation from legitimately qualified professionals and thereby pollute professional reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/philanthropic imposture soliciting funds
rubrics_metrics.description: 'TO THE LORD'S PEOPLE.— A dear Christian tradesman... is now in WANT OF FORTY POUNDS... The smallest help will be gratefully acknowledged by the Advertiser.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals framed in religious language to solicit money (false sanctity). The page calls this the 'foulest and nastiest' class of advertiser, noting their willingness to exploit faith and pity; warns that such adverts can be thinly veiled frauds (e.g., borrowing, deposits, or outright theft).

rubrics_metrics.name: Loan-office advertisements and inquiry-fee scams
rubrics_metrics.description: Loan-office advertisers... promise money without security. Now and again temporary offices are started... for the purpose of bagging the inquiry fees, and with no intention whatever of lending money. Their general ultimatum is, 'Security offered insufficient.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pattern: adverts promising unsecured loans or requesting inquiry/deposit fees; temporary/rumored offices set up to collect fees and disappear. The page advises skepticism: genuine money-lenders will insist on security and interest; 'temporary offices' are often fraudulent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper circulation fraud (fake circulation guarantees)
rubrics_metrics.description: the swindle of the newspaper proprietor who guarantees a circulation which has no existence... there are in London... papers that have absolutely no circulation, in the proper sense of the word, whatever; and of which only a sufficient number of copies is printed to supply those who advertise in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspaper proprietors guaranteeing and charging for non-existent or artificially small circulations; producing titles for advertisers rather than readers. The page documents the practice (multiple paper titles printed as one) and labels it a 'deliberate and barefaced robbery' of advertisers who pay for reach that doesn't exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufactured notoriety / paid puffery
rubrics_metrics.description: still more distinct... certain ambitious persons try to obtain a spurious notoriety... Literature and the various phases of art suffer most from these impostors... No one can be blind to the manner in which some very small literary lights manage to keep their names continually paraded before the public; and the puffs are so worded that the unthinking are bound to believe...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using paid or manufactured positive notices ('puffs') to create the illusion of fame or merit. The page identifies this as a swindle that passes off inferior works or persons as noteworthy and critiques publishers who prefer 'men with names' over merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading photographic advertising of performers
rubrics_metrics.description: At certain theatres shameless women... get themselves photographed in the most extraordinary attitudes, and their counterfeit presentments leer out from the shop windows... in a leading thoroughfare, of twenty-five English portraits exhibited in a window as those of actresses... there were not five that were really what they pretended to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of posed or deceptive photographs to imply stage credentials or entice audiences; mixing celebrated actresses' portraits with images of courtesans and minor performers, thereby misleading the public about performers' status and skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hoax spectacles / impossible-performance advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: AT the New Theatre in the Hay market... he... goes into [a common wine bottle] in the sight of all the Spectators, and sings in it; during his stay in the bottle, any Person may handle it, and see plainly that it does not exceed a common Tavern Bottle... Stage, 7s. 6d....
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising impossibly sensational feats (the 'bottle-trick' and similar claims) to attract crowds and money. The page shows how such hoaxes exploit gullibility, provoke public outrage when unfulfilled, and can cause riots and property destruction; also documents post-hoax self-defenses and satirical responses in the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploitation of grief and private-secrets claims (spirit mediumship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Note. — If any Gentlemen or Ladies... is desirous of seeing a representation of any deceased Person... upon making a gratuity to the Performer, shall be gratified... likewise, if desired, he will tell you your most secret thoughts in your past Life...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offering private sittings, seances, or revelations about deceased persons and 'secret thoughts' for gratuities. The page treats such offers as exploitative commercial tricks that prey on emotional vulnerability and charge for purported private revelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: False endorsements and extravagant testimonial claims
rubrics_metrics.description: These performances have been seen by most of the crowned Heads of Asia, Africa, and Europe, and never appeared public any where but once; but will wait on any at their Houses, and perform as above, for five Pounds each time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of grandiose or likely-fabricated endorsements (royalty, foreign courts) and exclusivity claims to convey legitimacy. The page cites such claims as typical puffery in adverts for spectacles and as a hallmark of fraudulent promotion.
